idiom_name: val properties with private backing fields and explicit backing fields
implementation_notes: Kotlin turns the pattern into a declaration choice: a `val` has a getter and no setter at all, and a constructor `val` parameter generates a private backing field plus a public accessor, so nothing outside the class can write it - a subclass cannot even widen it, because a `var` cannot override a `val`. For values that stay readable but legitimately change internally, `var` with `private set` is the escape hatch, and explicit backing fields or a backing property (`private val _users` with a read-only public view) give a read-only surface over mutable state. A separate data holder is justified only when several fields must be validated and copied as one unit; Kotlin then uses a private `data class` or a nested value class, with the copy done in its constructor.
pitfalls: `val` fixes the reference, not the contents: a `val list = mutableListOf<String>()` is still mutable, so expose `List<T>` (the read-only interface) or copies.
`internal` is not private - it becomes public in bytecode with mangled names - and `lateinit`/`@JvmField` properties expose their backing field to Java, so library boundaries need `private`.
A `var` with `private set` still allows the class itself to reassign the value; if the state must be frozen after construction, `val` plus a new instance is the honest form.
